stories.title: Research on Bayesian network probabilistic assessment model for soil seismic liquefaction considering small-sample and incomplete SPT data
stories.description: Liquefaction assessment is a critical task in seismic geotechnical engineering; however, existing methods are often limited by their reliance on complete datasets and inability to effectively handle missing information. This study proposes a Bayesian network-based framework for probabilistic liquefaction assessment under conditions of small sample size and incomplete Standard Penetration Test (SPT) data. Causal logical relationships derived from liquefaction mechanisms are incorporated to construct interpretable network structures. A systematic experimental framework integrating different parameter learning algorithms, training strategies, and missing-data handling schemes is developed to evaluate model performance under varying conditions. The results illustrate that small-sample models show limited performance, whereas incorporating incomplete information significantly improves prediction accuracy. Under the optimal combination of the real-sample-based training strategy (Method-1) and the maximum a posteriori probability (MAP)-based missing-data handling scheme (Scheme II), the five-factor Bayesian network model achieved an Overall Accuracy (OA), Precision (Pre), Recall (Rec), and F1-score (F1) of 80.56%, 74.00%, 97.37%, and 84.09%, respectively, on the independent validation dataset. It demonstrates the reliable predictive capability of the proposed model for unseen liquefaction cases. The proposed framework expands the applicability of probabilistic liquefaction assessment across different depth ranges, seismic loading conditions, and soil properties. Moreover, it provides an interpretable and robust solution for engineering scenarios where data incompleteness is unavoidable, offering practical value for seismic hazard assessment.

stories.title: Expansion of North Atlantic Deep Water during Northern Hemisphere Glaciation
stories.description: Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major driver of the Earth’s climate, moving heat from the Southern Hemisphere to the Northern Hemisphere. Neither foraminiferal carbon isotope records nor modelling studies agree on the spatial extent of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), the northern deep limb of the AMOC, over the intensification of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (iNHG, ~2.73 million years ago). Here we present high-resolution neodymium isotope (εNd) records from a depth transect in the equatorial Atlantic over the iNHG. We find a persistent latitudinal and depth gradient in neodymium isotope values in the deep Atlantic during the Late Pliocene, absent in the Early Pleistocene, indicating an expansion of NADW extent over the iNHG. In contrast, our reconstruction suggests very little glacial-interglacial variability in NADW extent during both the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene. These results suggest deep-water circulation was substantially different during a warm climate state, with implications for the role of NADW formation during major climate transitions and its future stability. As the climate transitioned from the warm Pliocene to the cooler Pleistocene (~3 Ma), the Atlantic Ocean deep circulation changed, with a permanent expansion of North Atlantic Deep Water, according to new neodymium isotope records.
